title: Japan — Northern Alps in autumn
notes: Fifteen nights, sequenced north to south and high to low so it follows the autumn colour down the mountain rather than fighting it, then two nights in Nagoya and a last one in Tokyo to finish on something other than mountains. The dates are a deliberate trade: Hakuba's alpine colour peaks late September, the Nakasendo's peaks late October, and five weeks apart they cannot both be caught in one trip — so this window takes the Kiso valley and Kamikochi's larch at their best and accepts Hakuba past its peak, with the colour down at the mid-mountain and the village. It also sits clear of the Sports Day holiday weekend entirely. Nothing is booked yet.

summary.note: Budget figures are the whole trip for two travellers, in MYR, and are planning estimates rather than quotes — nothing is booked. They exclude flights. The exchange rate is the mid-market rate on 14 Aug 2026 (1 MYR = 38.9 JPY), a placeholder until money is actually changed; every converted figure on the site moves with it. Day costs carry only fares that have been looked up and checked, as a group total for two, so the daily totals are well below what a day will really cost — the planning envelope is this table, not those. Shopping is deliberately not here and is tracked separately; Miscellaneous is contingency, not a shopping allowance.

flights.remarks: Not booked. Times are ANA's current timetable as at Aug 2026, held as the planning baseline until the October 2027 schedule loads (usually around 11 months out, so roughly Nov 2026). Waiting on an ANA promotion.

overview.remarks: Placed after Okuhida rather than before it for one reason: the larch turns golden roughly 25 Oct to 5 Nov, about a week behind the maples, and today is the leading edge of that. Coming here before Okuhida would land on the 21st, which falls between the two — maples going over, larch not yet started. Private cars are banned in the valley; bus or taxi only.

A deliberate change of register for the last three nights: city, food and trains rather than more mountains. Note that Nagoya's own autumn colour does not peak until late November, so this block is not about leaves.

The one full day in Nagoya, so it is the city rather than a day trip. Swapping the whole day for Inuyama (an original castle and the Meiji Mura open-air museum, 30 minutes out by Meitetsu) or Ghibli Park is the alternative — but it is one or the other now, not both.

Back to Tokyo a night early so the last day is shopping rather than travelling. The hotel is deliberately on the Haneda side — the Nozomi from Nagoya stops at Shinagawa, so there is no need to carry bags on to Tokyo Station and back out again.

accommodation.remarks: Airport hotel — the flight lands at 22:15, so anything further in wastes a night.
Three nights on one base. Ask about laundry — this and Okuhida are the two longest stops.
Near the castle or the station both work; Nakamachi is the nicer evening walk.
Shin-Hotaka or Fukuji. A private or semi-open rotenburo is the whole point of these three nights, so pick for the bath rather than the room.
Book this first. Fewer than ten properties inside the valley and late October sells out months ahead. Half board is the norm — there is nowhere else to eat after dark.
Edo-era minshuku in the post town itself. Late October is the busiest stretch of the year on the Nakasendo and the houses are small, so book early.
Anywhere around Nagoya Station or Sakae. The station is the better base — the shinkansen out leaves from it, and the food arcades are underneath.

Shinagawa is the pick: every Nozomi from Nagoya stops there, the Keikyu runs to Haneda in about 15 minutes, and Ginza and Shibuya are both inside a quarter of an hour. Hamamatsucho is the equivalent on the monorail side. Confirm at check-in that they will hold the bags after checkout — standard and usually free, but the whole last day is built on it.

transport.mode: Trains, buses, gondolas and ropeways throughout — no hire car. Private vehicles are banned in Kamikochi, and nothing else on the route needs one.
